claim: Schistosomiasis is a debilitating parasitic disease infecting hundreds of millions of people.
source: Schistosomiasis is a debilitating parasitic disease infecting hundreds of millions of people.
evidence: Supported by citations to Evan Secor, 2014 and Lo et al., 2018 in the manuscript text

claim: Schistosomes use aquatic snails as intermediate hosts.
source: Schistosomes use aquatic snails as intermediate hosts.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lo et al., 2018 in the manuscript text

claim: PTC2 exhibits the largest known correlation with susceptibility to parasite infection with over 15 fold effect.
source: In a genome-wide association study of Biomphalaria glabrata snails, we identify genomic region PTC2 which exhibits the largest known correlation with susceptibility to parasite infection (>15 fold effect).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from genome-wide association study and genotyping experiments showing infection odds differences

claim: PTC2 haplotypes are exceptionally divergent in structure and sequence.
source: Using new genome assemblies with substantially higher contiguity than the Biomphalaria reference genome, we show that PTC2 haplotypes are exceptionally divergent in structure and sequence.
evidence: Supported by PacBio assembly data showing structural variation and sequence divergence

claim: PTC2 variation includes multi-kilobase indels containing entire genes.
source: This variation includes multi-kilobase indels containing entire genes, and orthologs for which most amino acid residues are polymorphic.
evidence: Supported by genome assembly data and annotation showing large insertions/deletions with complete genes

claim: Most PTC2 genes encode single-pass transmembrane proteins.
source: RNA-Seq annotation reveals that most of these genes encode single-pass transmembrane proteins, as seen in another resistance region in the same species.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data and protein structure prediction showing transmembrane domains

claim: Over 200 million people worldwide suffer from schistosomiasis.
source: Schistosomiasis is a chronic and debilitating disease suffered by over 200 million people worldwide (Evan Secor, 2014; Lo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Evan Secor, 2014 and Lo et al., 2018

claim: Schistosomiasis is caused by infection with schistosome trematode parasites that are transmitted by aquatic snails.
source: It is caused by infection with schistosome trematode parasites that are transmitted by aquatic snails (Lo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lo et al., 2018

claim: Schistosome infection can be treated with regular doses of praziquantel.
source: Infection can be treated with regular doses of a single drug, praziquantel (Doenhoff et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doenhoff et al., 2009

claim: Mass drug administration alone will not adequately control schistosomiasis.
source: However, it has become increasingly clear that mass drug administration alone will not adequately control schistosomiasis, and that successful elimination of transmission requires intervention at the snail stage (Lo et al., 2018; Sokolow et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lo et al., 2018 and Sokolow et al., 2018

claim: Successful elimination of schistosomiasis transmission requires intervention at the snail stage.
source: However, it has become increasingly clear that mass drug administration alone will not adequately control schistosomiasis, and that successful elimination of transmission requires intervention at the snail stage (Lo et al., 2018; Sokolow et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lo et al., 2018 and Sokolow et al., 2018

claim: Parasite resistance is highly heritable in snails.
source: Parasite resistance is highly heritable in snails, and there is substantial strain-by-strain interaction between hosts and parasites (Richards and Shade, 1987; Richards et al., 1992; Knight et al., 1999; Webster et al., 2004; Webster and Woolhouse, 1998; Theron et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting heritability of resistance

claim: There is substantial strain-by-strain interaction between snail hosts and schistosome parasites.
source: Parasite resistance is highly heritable in snails, and there is substantial strain-by-strain interaction between hosts and parasites (Richards and Shade, 1987; Richards et al., 1992; Knight et al., 1999; Webster et al., 2004; Webster and Woolhouse, 1998; Theron et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting strain-specific interactions

claim: Genetically diverse parasite cultures can infect nearly all snails.
source: Genetically diverse parasite cultures can infect nearly all snails, while bottlenecked laboratory strains of parasite can only infect a subset (Theron et al., 2008), suggesting a 'trench warfare' model in which numerous alleles are maintained in both host and parasite populations because each matches a different phenotype in the other species (Seger, 1988; Stahl et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Theron et al., 2008

claim: Bottlenecked laboratory strains of parasite can only infect a subset of snails.
source: Genetically diverse parasite cultures can infect nearly all snails, while bottlenecked laboratory strains of parasite can only infect a subset (Theron et al., 2008), suggesting a 'trench warfare' model in which numerous alleles are maintained in both host and parasite populations because each matches a different phenotype in the other species (Seger, 1988; Stahl et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Theron et al., 2008

claim: There are likely to be snail genes with large effects on resistance to particular parasite genotypes.
source: There are likely to be snail genes with large effects on resistance to particular parasite genotypes (Lewis et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lewis et al., 2001 and inference from genetic data

claim: The Biomphalaria glabrata reference genome BglaB1 has an N50 of 48 kb.
source: The neotropical snail Biomphalaria glabrata has been the focus of recent efforts to develop genomic resources for schistosomiasis vector biology, although the 916 Mb, repetitive genome remains poorly assembled (reference genome BglaB1 N50 = 48 kb; Adema et al., 2017; Tennessen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adema et al., 2017 and Tennessen et al., 2017

claim: The Biomphalaria glabrata genome is 916 Mb in size.
source: The neotropical snail Biomphalaria glabrata has been the focus of recent efforts to develop genomic resources for schistosomiasis vector biology, although the 916 Mb, repetitive genome remains poorly assembled (reference genome BglaB1 N50 = 48 kb; Adema et al., 2017; Tennessen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adema et al., 2017 and Tennessen et al., 2017

claim: Four genomic regions have been identified in which allelic variation influences resistance to infection by S. mansoni in B. glabrata.
source: To date, four genomic regions have been identified in which allelic variation influences resistance to infection by S. mansoni (Knight et al., 1999; Goodall et al., 2006; Tennessen et al., 2015a; Tennessen et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies identifying resistance loci

claim: An F2 mapping cross between resistant B. glabrata strain BS-90 and a susceptible strain yielded two RAPD markers linked to resistance.
source: An F2 mapping cross between resistant B. glabrata strain BS-90 and a susceptible strain yielded two RAPD markers linked to resistance (Knight et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knight et al., 1999

claim: One BS-90 RAPD marker was subsequently aligned to a contig on Linkage Group XII.
source: One of those was subsequently aligned to a contig on Linkage Group (LG) XII (Tennessen et al., 2017), although the identities of any candidate genes to which it may be linked remain unclear (the other could not be uniquely mapped).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tennessen et al., 2017

claim: The sod1 and RADres genomic regions together explain only 7% of the variance in resistance in population 13-16-R1.
source: However, together those two regions explain only 7% of the variance in resistance in 13-16-R1, suggesting that other resistance loci remain undiscovered in this population.
evidence: Supported by data from previous genetic analysis

claim: The Guadeloupe Resistance Complex (GRC) shows an 8-fold effect on the odds of S. mansoni infection.
source: In B. glabrata from Guadeloupe, the Guadeloupe Resistance Complex (GRC) shows an 8-fold effect on the odds of S. mansoni infection (Tennessen et al., 2015b; Allan et al., 2017) via a hemocyte-mediated mechanism (Allan et al., 2018a) that also affects the proteome (Allan et al., 2019) and microbiome (Allan et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tennessen et al., 2015b and Allan et al., 2017

claim: GRC functions via a hemocyte-mediated mechanism.
source: In B. glabrata from Guadeloupe, the Guadeloupe Resistance Complex (GRC) shows an 8-fold effect on the odds of S. mansoni infection (Tennessen et al., 2015b; Allan et al., 2017) via a hemocyte-mediated mechanism (Allan et al., 2018a) that also affects the proteome (Allan et al., 2019) and microbiome (Allan et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Allan et al., 2018a

claim: Seven clustered GRC genes encode hyperdiverse single-pass transmembrane proteins.
source: Seven clustered GRC genes encode hyperdiverse single-pass transmembrane (TM1) proteins that appear to recognize parasite-associated molecules (Tennessen et al., 2015b), likely including saccharides (Allan and Blouin, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tennessen et al., 2015b

claim: GRC proteins appear to recognize parasite-associated molecules.
source: Seven clustered GRC genes encode hyperdiverse single-pass transmembrane (TM1) proteins that appear to recognize parasite-associated molecules (Tennessen et al., 2015b), likely including saccharides (Allan and Blouin, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tennessen et al., 2015b and Allan and Blouin, 2018

claim: A single genomic region on LG XII showed by far the greatest difference in allele frequencies between infected and uninfected snail pools.
source: In pooled whole-genome sequencing of 600 infected and 600 uninfected 13–16-R1 snails (298x and 333x coverage, respectively), a single genomic region showed by far the greatest difference in allele frequencies between pools (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Supported by pooled sequencing data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The highest outliers in allele frequency differences occurred in a 450 kb section of LG XII called PTC2.
source: The highest outliers occurred in a 450 kb section of LG XII, here called PTC2.
evidence: Supported by pooled sequencing data analysis

claim: Genetic divergence (FST) at numerous PTC2 variants exceeds 0.1.
source: Genetic divergence between pools (FST) at numerous PTC2 variants exceeds 0.1, a value unobserved among one billion simulated neutral variants, which is therefore significant even if corrected for the nearly 7 million empirical variants examined (p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by FST calculations from pooled sequencing data and simulation analysis

claim: FST exceeding 0.1 at PTC2 is significant even after correction for multiple testing (p<0.01).
source: Genetic divergence between pools (FST) at numerous PTC2 variants exceeds 0.1, a value unobserved among one billion simulated neutral variants, which is therefore significant even if corrected for the nearly 7 million empirical variants examined (p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by simulation analysis showing this FST value is unlikely under neutrality

claim: Many PTC2 variants show FST over 0.2.
source: Many variants even show FST over 0.2, more than twice the FST at sod1 and RADres.
evidence: Supported by FST calculations from pooled sequencing data

claim: Three PTC2 alleles exist at intermediate frequency: R (44%), S1 (24%), and S2 (32%).
source: By subsequently genotyping indel polymorphisms at PTC2 in individual snails, we observed three alleles at intermediate frequency (R: 44%, S1: 24%, and S2: 32%).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data from individual snails

claim: Infection was rare for RR homozygotes (12.9%).
source: Infection was rare for RR homozygotes (12.9%), and much more common for S1S1 (75.3%) and S2S2 (29.6%) homozygotes, a difference in infection odds of over 15-fold (i.e. infection odds of 0.15 vs. 3.0; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by phenotyping and genotyping data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Infection was much more common for S1S1 homozygotes (75.3%).
source: Infection was rare for RR homozygotes (12.9%), and much more common for S1S1 (75.3%) and S2S2 (29.6%) homozygotes, a difference in infection odds of over 15-fold (i.e. infection odds of 0.15 vs. 3.0; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by phenotyping and genotyping data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Infection was common for S2S2 homozygotes (29.6%).
source: Infection was rare for RR homozygotes (12.9%), and much more common for S1S1 (75.3%) and S2S2 (29.6%) homozygotes, a difference in infection odds of over 15-fold (i.e. infection odds of 0.15 vs. 3.0; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by phenotyping and genotyping data shown in Figure 1B

claim: There is a difference in infection odds of over 15-fold between RR and S1S1 genotypes.
source: Infection was rare for RR homozygotes (12.9%), and much more common for S1S1 (75.3%) and S2S2 (29.6%) homozygotes, a difference in infection odds of over 15-fold (i.e. infection odds of 0.15 vs. 3.0; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by phenotyping and genotyping data shown in Figure 1B

claim: PTC2 heterozygotes showed intermediate infection phenotypes.
source: Heterozygotes showed intermediate phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by phenotyping data from heterozygous individuals

claim: There is weak partial dominance of S1 over R at PTC2.
source: There was weak partial dominance of S1 over R (observed Clopper-Pearson 95% confidence interval of infection probability for S1R = 51.0–61.8%; expected intermediate phenotype = 44.1%), such that relative to RR, carrying an S1 allele increases the odds of infection 5.9-fold (p=6 × 10−42) while a second S1 allele further increases the odds of infection 2.7-fold for a 15.9-fold difference (p=1 × 10−4).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of genotype-phenotype associations

claim: Carrying an S1 allele increases the odds of infection 5.9-fold relative to RR (p=6 × 10−42).
source: There was weak partial dominance of S1 over R (observed Clopper-Pearson 95% confidence interval of infection probability for S1R = 51.0–61.8%; expected intermediate phenotype = 44.1%), such that relative to RR, carrying an S1 allele increases the odds of infection 5.9-fold (p=6 × 10−42) while a second S1 allele further increases the odds of infection 2.7-fold for a 15.9-fold difference (p=1 × 10−4).
evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of genotype-phenotype data

claim: A second S1 allele further increases the odds of infection 2.7-fold (p=1 × 10−4).
source: There was weak partial dominance of S1 over R (observed Clopper-Pearson 95% confidence interval of infection probability for S1R = 51.0–61.8%; expected intermediate phenotype = 44.1%), such that relative to RR, carrying an S1 allele increases the odds of infection 5.9-fold (p=6 × 10−42) while a second S1 allele further increases the odds of infection 2.7-fold for a 15.9-fold difference (p=1 × 10−4).
evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of genotype-phenotype data

claim: The S2 allele acts additively, with each S2 allele increasing the odds of infection 1.5-fold (p=6 × 10−5).
source: The S2 allele acts additively, such that each S2 allele increases the odds of infection 1.5-fold (p=6 × 10−5).
evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of genotype-phenotype data

claim: The PTC2 signal was confirmed using an independent set of 392 snails from 13-16-R1.
source: We confirmed the PTC2 signal using an independent set of 392 snails from 13-16-R1 that had previously been phenotyped (Tennessen et al., 2015a) (p=7 × 10−12 for R vs. S1; p=4 × 10−5 for R vs. S2; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by genotyping and phenotyping data from independent sample set

claim: All three loci (PTC2, sod1, and RADres) had significant independent associations when included together in the same model (p≤10−4 for each).
source: These snails had also been genotyped at sod1 and RADres, revealing that all three loci had significant independent associations when included together in the same model (p≤10−4 for each), with no evidence for epistasis (p>0.05 for interaction terms).
evidence: Supported by multi-locus logistic regression analysis

claim: There is no evidence for epistasis among PTC2, sod1, and RADres (p>0.05 for interaction terms).
source: These snails had also been genotyped at sod1 and RADres, revealing that all three loci had significant independent associations when included together in the same model (p≤10−4 for each), with no evidence for epistasis (p>0.05 for interaction terms).
evidence: Supported by multi-locus logistic regression analysis testing interaction terms

claim: Segregating variation at PTC2 has a stronger association with odds of infection than that of any other known B. glabrata locus.
source: Segregating variation at PTC2 has a stronger association with odds of infection than that of any other known B. glabrata locus (Tennessen et al., 2015a; Tennessen et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by comparison of effect sizes across known resistance loci

claim: The BS-90 RAPD marker is 5 Mb and 23 cM from PTC2.
source: The BS-90 RAPD marker (Knight et al., 1999) is only 5 Mb and 23 cM from PTC2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Tennessen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by genome assembly and linkage map data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The BS-90 RAPD marker is predicted to be 17 cM (range 6–33 cM) from a causal locus.
source: This marker is predicted to be 17 cM (range 6–33 cM) from a causal locus, which could therefore plausibly be PTC2 (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by statistical inference from mapping data

claim: Alignable regions of PTC2 haplotypes show 3.3% nucleotide divergence on average (SD = 2.1%).
source: Alignable regions show 3.3% nucleotide divergence on average (SD = 2.1%).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis of PacBio assemblies

claim: A majority of PTC2 sequence shows no similarity among alleles.
source: A majority of PTC2 sequence shows no similarity among alleles; the percentage of sequence that could even be aligned ranged from 12.9% (R onto S2) to 40.0% (S1 onto R).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis of PacBio assemblies

claim: The percentage of PTC2 sequence that could be aligned ranged from 12.9% (R onto S2) to 40.0% (S1 onto R).
source: A majority of PTC2 sequence shows no similarity among alleles; the percentage of sequence that could even be aligned ranged from 12.9% (R onto S2) to 40.0% (S1 onto R).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis of PacBio assemblies

claim: All three PTC2 haplotypes harbor unique insertions tens of thousands of bp in size.
source: All three PTC2 haplotypes harbor unique insertions tens of thousands of bp in size, some of which contain complete coding genes, such that each genotype carries a distinct combination of genes (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by genome assembly and annotation data shown in Figure 2

claim: Each PTC2 genotype carries a distinct combination of genes.
source: All three PTC2 haplotypes harbor unique insertions tens of thousands of bp in size, some of which contain complete coding genes, such that each genotype carries a distinct combination of genes (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by genome assembly and annotation data shown in Figure 2

claim: Shared orthologous genes at PTC2 show many nonsynonymous differences.
source: Shared orthologous genes at PTC2 show many nonsynonymous differences and in some cases homology can only be identified at the protein, not DNA, level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and protein alignments shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: For some PTC2 genes, homology can only be identified at the protein level, not DNA level.
source: Shared orthologous genes at PTC2 show many nonsynonymous differences and in some cases homology can only be identified at the protein, not DNA, level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3

claim: The degree of polymorphism at PTC2 is unusually high for conspecific haplotypes in most genomic regions in any taxon.
source: This degree of polymorphism is unusually high for conspecific haplotypes in most genomic regions in any taxon (Leffler et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by comparison to literature on genomic diversity

claim: Outside of PTC2, 89.5% of sequence can be aligned between assemblies, with a mean of 0.4% nucleotide divergence.
source: In contrast to PTC2, 89.5% of sequence on other contigs can be aligned between assemblies, with a mean of 0.4% nucleotide divergence.
evidence: Supported by genome-wide sequence alignment analysis

claim: PTC2 contains eleven genes.
source: Using RNA-Seq data from homozygotes of each genotype to identify expressed genes, we fully annotated PTC2 (Supplementary file 1D,E). Of the eleven PTC2 genes, eight are predicted to be TM1 genes, including all five genes that are shared among the three haplotypes (genes 1, 2, 4, 5, and 9; Figure 2; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq annotation data

claim: Eight of the eleven PTC2 genes are predicted to be TM1 genes.
source: Using RNA-Seq data from homozygotes of each genotype to identify expressed genes, we fully annotated PTC2 (Supplementary file 1D,E). Of the eleven PTC2 genes, eight are predicted to be TM1 genes, including all five genes that are shared among the three haplotypes (genes 1, 2, 4, 5, and 9; Figure 2; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq annotation and protein structure prediction

claim: All five genes shared among the three PTC2 haplotypes are TM1 genes.
source: Using RNA-Seq data from homozygotes of each genotype to identify expressed genes, we fully annotated PTC2 (Supplementary file 1D,E). Of the eleven PTC2 genes, eight are predicted to be TM1 genes, including all five genes that are shared among the three haplotypes (genes 1, 2, 4, 5, and 9; Figure 2; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq annotation and protein structure prediction shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: Only 11% of B. glabrata genes are TM1 genes.
source: Only 11% of B. glabrata genes are TM1 genes, so they would be unlikely to constitute eight of eleven genes by chance alone (p<10−5).
evidence: Supported by genome-wide annotation analysis

claim: TM1 genes would be unlikely to constitute eight of eleven PTC2 genes by chance alone (p<10−5).
source: Only 11% of B. glabrata genes are TM1 genes, so they would be unlikely to constitute eight of eleven genes by chance alone (p<10−5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis comparing observed to expected gene composition

claim: PTC2 TM1 genes are all between 166 and 530 codons.
source: PTC2 TM1 genes are all between 166 and 530 codons, have TM1 domains that are displaced from the N-terminus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and like the rest of PTC2 they are highly polymorphic (Figure 3), with amino acid level divergence exceeding 50% in several cases.
evidence: Supported by gene annotation data

claim: PTC2 TM1 genes have TM1 domains that are displaced from the N-terminus.
source: PTC2 TM1 genes are all between 166 and 530 codons, have TM1 domains that are displaced from the N-terminus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and like the rest of PTC2 they are highly polymorphic (Figure 3), with amino acid level divergence exceeding 50% in several cases.
evidence: Supported by protein structure analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: PTC2 TM1 genes show amino acid level divergence exceeding 50% in several cases.
source: PTC2 TM1 genes are all between 166 and 530 codons, have TM1 domains that are displaced from the N-terminus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and like the rest of PTC2 they are highly polymorphic (Figure 3), with amino acid level divergence exceeding 50% in several cases.
evidence: Supported by protein sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3

claim: Sequences similar to both R and S haplotypes are present in other B. glabrata populations without admixed histories.
source: Sequences similar to both R and S haplotypes are present in other B. glabrata populations without admixed histories (genomic and transcriptomic sequence from Brazilian strain BB02, Adema et al., 2017; transcriptomic sequence from Guadeloupe, Tennessen et al., 2015b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that they co-occur throughout the species range and the polymorphism is old.
evidence: Supported by sequence data from multiple populations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: PTC2 alleles co-occur throughout the B. glabrata species range.
source: Sequences similar to both R and S haplotypes are present in other B. glabrata populations without admixed histories (genomic and transcriptomic sequence from Brazilian strain BB02, Adema et al., 2017; transcriptomic sequence from Guadeloupe, Tennessen et al., 2015b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that they co-occur throughout the species range and the polymorphism is old.
evidence: Supported by sequence data from geographically diverse populations

claim: The PTC2 polymorphism is old.
source: Sequences similar to both R and S haplotypes are present in other B. glabrata populations without admixed histories (genomic and transcriptomic sequence from Brazilian strain BB02, Adema et al., 2017; transcriptomic sequence from Guadeloupe, Tennessen et al., 2015b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that they co-occur throughout the species range and the polymorphism is old.
evidence: Inferred from presence of similar alleles across geographically diverse populations

claim: Synonymous divergence among PTC2 alleles is higher than nonsynonymous divergence.
source: Synonymous divergence among alleles is higher than nonsynonymous, and a phylogeny of concatenated genes shows 24% synonymous divergence from the midpoint root.
evidence: Supported by sequence divergence analysis

claim: A phylogeny of concatenated PTC2 genes shows 24% synonymous divergence from the midpoint root.
source: Synonymous divergence among alleles is higher than nonsynonymous, and a phylogeny of concatenated genes shows 24% synonymous divergence from the midpoint root.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis of concatenated gene sequences

claim: PTC2 haplotypes are more consistent with an ancient origin (24 million years assuming a neutral mutation rate of 10−8 per year) rather than recent divergence via selection for protein diversity.
source: Thus, haplotypes are more consistent with an ancient origin (24 million years assuming a neutral mutation rate of 10−8 per year) rather than recent divergence via selection for protein diversity.
evidence: Inferred from synonymous divergence data and molecular clock assumptions

claim: PTC2 genes contain no known protein domains or homology to sequences outside of gastropods, other than the transmembrane segment.
source: Other than the transmembrane segment, these genes contain no known protein domains or homology to sequences outside of gastropods, nor are they homologous to GRC genes.
evidence: Supported by protein domain analysis and sequence homology searches

claim: PTC2 genes are not homologous to GRC genes.
source: Other than the transmembrane segment, these genes contain no known protein domains or homology to sequences outside of gastropods, nor are they homologous to GRC genes.
evidence: Supported by sequence homology analysis

claim: Some PTC2 genes show homology to each other and/or to other genes near PTC2 or elsewhere in the genome.
source: Some show homology to each other and/or to other genes near PTC2 or elsewhere in the genome, but amino acid level sequence similarity among paralogs is low (<50%).
evidence: Supported by sequence homology analysis

claim: Amino acid level sequence similarity among PTC2 paralogs is low (<50%).
source: Some show homology to each other and/or to other genes near PTC2 or elsewhere in the genome, but amino acid level sequence similarity among paralogs is low (<50%).
evidence: Supported by protein sequence alignment analysis

claim: Both GRC and PTC2 suggest a model of snail-schistosome interaction via molecular recognition mediated by TM1 gene polymorphism.
source: Both GRC and PTC2 suggest a model of snail-schistosome interaction via molecular recognition (either of the parasite by the host, or of the host by the parasite) that is mediated by TM1 gene polymorphism.
evidence: Inferred from the shared features of GRC and PTC2 (both contain polymorphic TM1 genes associated with resistance)

claim: Across metazoans, TM1 genes often play a role in immunological recognition.
source: Across metazoans, TM1 genes often play a role in immunological recognition, and include B- and T-cell receptors, Toll-like receptors, major histocompatibility complex genes, and similar host defense genes (Pahl et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pahl et al., 2013

claim: Polymorphic clusters of host transmembrane genes are used by parasites as receptors for host recognition and invasion.
source: Other polymorphic clusters of host transmembrane genes are used by parasites as receptors for host recognition and invasion (e.g. human glycophorins and Plasmodium; Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al., 2017), and at least one of the GRC TM1 genes controls shedding of S. mansoni cercariae (Allan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al., 2017 and Allan et al., 2017

claim: At least one of the GRC TM1 genes controls shedding of S. mansoni cercariae.
source: Other polymorphic clusters of host transmembrane genes are used by parasites as receptors for host recognition and invasion (e.g. human glycophorins and Plasmodium; Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al., 2017), and at least one of the GRC TM1 genes controls shedding of S. mansoni cercariae (Allan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Allan et al., 2017

claim: In contrast to GRC, all three PTC2 alleles differ in their susceptibility.
source: In contrast to GRC, in which a completely dominant allele confers resistance, all three alleles in PTC2 differ in their susceptibility, and allelic associations are additive or show partial dominant susceptibility (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by genotype-phenotype association data shown in Figure 1B

claim: PTC2 allelic associations are additive or show partial dominant susceptibility.
source: In contrast to GRC, in which a completely dominant allele confers resistance, all three alleles in PTC2 differ in their susceptibility, and allelic associations are additive or show partial dominant susceptibility (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of genotype-phenotype associations

claim: Multiple loci along the PTC2 haplotypes may jointly contribute to phenotype by interacting with different combinations of parasite molecules.
source: This pattern suggests that multiple loci along the haplotypes may jointly contribute to phenotype by interacting with different combinations of parasite molecules such as SmPoMucs (Roger et al., 2008) or other glycoproteins (Allan and Blouin, 2018) to determine the outcome of infection.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of allelic effects and comparison to known parasite molecules

claim: The inferred ancient origin of PTC2 (>20 million years) is inconsistent with a neutral coalescent process.
source: The inferred ancient origin (>20 million years) of PTC2 is inconsistent with a neutral coalescent process.
evidence: Inferred from molecular clock analysis and population genetic theory

claim: The remarkable structural and nonsynonymous polymorphism at PTC2 appears adaptive.
source: Therefore, while the remarkable structural and nonsynonymous polymorphism appears adaptive, it is difficult to distinguish among plausible scenarios including overdominance (Woolhouse et al., 2002), negative-frequency dependent selection (Woolhouse et al., 2002; Koskella and Lively, 2009; Bento et al., 2017), adaptive introgression from distantly related species (Hedrick, 2013), or selection for an epistatically-interacting supergene (Thompson and Jiggins, 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the patterns of polymorphism and ancient divergence

claim: Adaptive introgression appears unlikely as an explanation for PTC2 polymorphism because it would have had to occur twice independently to generate three distinct haplotypes.
source: Introgression appears unlikely, as it would have had to occur twice independently to generate three distinct haplotypes, and all of the closest relatives of B. glabrata occur allopatrically in Africa (DeJong et al., 2001).
evidence: Inferred from the number of haplotypes and biogeography

claim: All of the closest relatives of B. glabrata occur allopatrically in Africa.
source: Introgression appears unlikely, as it would have had to occur twice independently to generate three distinct haplotypes, and all of the closest relatives of B. glabrata occur allopatrically in Africa (DeJong et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to DeJong et al., 2001

claim: The most plausible explanations for PTC2 polymorphism involve some form of long-term balancing selection.
source: Therefore, the most plausible explanations involve some form of long-term balancing selection.
evidence: Inferred from elimination of other scenarios and patterns of ancient polymorphism

claim: S. mansoni is not native to the neotropics.
source: Although S. mansoni is not native to the neotropics (Desprès et al., 1993), selection may have been driven by other trematodes, a clade that has ubiquitously infected snails for millions of years (Blair et al., 2001) and which can be a strong selective force favoring rare alleles (Koskella and Lively, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Desprès et al., 1993

claim: Trematodes have ubiquitously infected snails for millions of years.
source: Although S. mansoni is not native to the neotropics (Desprès et al., 1993), selection may have been driven by other trematodes, a clade that has ubiquitously infected snails for millions of years (Blair et al., 2001) and which can be a strong selective force favoring rare alleles (Koskella and Lively, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blair et al., 2001

claim: Trematodes can be a strong selective force favoring rare alleles in snails.
source: Although S. mansoni is not native to the neotropics (Desprès et al., 1993), selection may have been driven by other trematodes, a clade that has ubiquitously infected snails for millions of years (Blair et al., 2001) and which can be a strong selective force favoring rare alleles (Koskella and Lively, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koskella and Lively, 2009

claim: Schistosomes castrate snails.
source: Schistosomes castrate snails (Faro et al., 2013) but wild snails show no sign of evolving universal resistance, suggesting that the R haplotype is either specific to parasite genotype or else costly to fitness in some undetected manner.
evidence: Supported by citation to Faro et al., 2013

claim: Wild snails show no sign of evolving universal resistance to schistosomes.
source: Schistosomes castrate snails (Faro et al., 2013) but wild snails show no sign of evolving universal resistance, suggesting that the R haplotype is either specific to parasite genotype or else costly to fitness in some undetected manner.
evidence: Inferred from the maintenance of susceptible alleles despite strong selection

claim: The R allele has persisted within the 13–16-R1 population for decades in the absence of challenge by parasites.
source: The R allele has persisted within the 13–16-R1 population for decades in the absence of challenge by parasites, so any fitness cost must be relatively weak or context-dependent.
evidence: Supported by knowledge of the laboratory population history

claim: Any fitness cost of the R allele must be relatively weak or context-dependent.
source: The R allele has persisted within the 13–16-R1 population for decades in the absence of challenge by parasites, so any fitness cost must be relatively weak or context-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of the R allele in the absence of parasites

claim: A system of polymorphic matching alleles could explain the substantial schistosome-strain by snail-strain interaction in compatibility.
source: Nevertheless, a system of polymorphic matching alleles could explain the substantial schistosome-strain by snail-strain interaction in compatibility that is often observed (Richards and Shade, 1987; Richards et al., 1992; Knight et al., 1999; Webster et al., 2004; Webster and Woolhouse, 1998; Theron et al., 2014), including schistosome-infection dose-response curves that fit a simple phenotype-matching model (Theron et al., 2008; Theron et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the patterns of polymorphism and supported by citations to studies showing strain-specific interactions

claim: Schistosome-infection dose-response curves fit a simple phenotype-matching model.
source: Nevertheless, a system of polymorphic matching alleles could explain the substantial schistosome-strain by snail-strain interaction in compatibility that is often observed (Richards and Shade, 1987; Richards et al., 1992; Knight et al., 1999; Webster et al., 2004; Webster and Woolhouse, 1998; Theron et al., 2014), including schistosome-infection dose-response curves that fit a simple phenotype-matching model (Theron et al., 2008; Theron et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Theron et al., 2008 and Theron et al., 2014

claim: The PR-locus mediating bacterial resistance in Daphnia features haplotypes of vastly different sizes with large non-homologous sections.
source: For example, the PR-locus mediating bacterial resistance in Daphnia via matching-allele interactions also features haplotypes of vastly different sizes (differences > 60 kb at both this locus and PTC2) with large non-homologous sections, and these contain glycosyltransferase genes that could mediate host-pathogen compatibility (Bento et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bento et al., 2017

claim: The APL1 immune factor impacting Plasmodium development in Anopheles consists of adjacent paralogs that differ in copy number among species and show extreme diversity within species.
source: Similarly, the APL1 immune factor impacting Plasmodium development in Anopheles consists of adjacent paralogs that differ in copy number among species and show extreme diversity within species (Rottschaefer et al., 2011; Mitri et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rottschaefer et al., 2011 and Mitri et al., 2020

claim: Invertebrates lack the acquired immunity of vertebrates and its associated adaptive genetic variation.
source: Thus, while invertebrates lack the acquired immunity of vertebrates and its associated adaptive genetic variation (Spurgin and Richardson, 2010), their defenses can show similar nuance conveyed by molecular diversity (Loker et al., 2004; Cerenius and Söderhäll, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Spurgin and Richardson, 2010

claim: Invertebrate defenses can show similar nuance to vertebrate immunity conveyed by molecular diversity.
source: Thus, while invertebrates lack the acquired immunity of vertebrates and its associated adaptive genetic variation (Spurgin and Richardson, 2010), their defenses can show similar nuance conveyed by molecular diversity (Loker et al., 2004; Cerenius and Söderhäll, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Loker et al., 2004 and Cerenius and Söderhäll, 2013

claim: For invertebrates, increased numbers of distinct immunogenetic sequences may not necessarily lead to increased resistance if parasites also use these sequences to recognize hosts or mount evasion strategies.
source: For invertebrates, increased numbers of distinct immunogenetic sequences may not necessarily lead to increased resistance if parasites also use these sequences to recognize hosts or mount evasion strategies (Schmid-Hempel, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmid-Hempel, 2005 and logical inference

claim: The successful implementation of CRISPR/Cas9 in gastropods will facilitate the creation of genetically modified snails having enhanced immunity.
source: The successful implementation of CRISPR/Cas9 in gastropods (Abe and Kuroda, 2019) will facilitate the creation of genetically modified snails having enhanced immunity to block disease transmission (Maier et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abe and Kuroda, 2019 and Maier et al., 2019

claim: TM1 clusters are excellent candidates to target in efforts to create genetically modified snails with enhanced immunity.
source: As large-effect loci, the TM1 clusters are excellent candidates to target in such efforts.
evidence: Inferred from the large effect sizes of TM1 clusters on resistance

claim: If host polymorphism is adaptive, it may not be readily replaced in natural populations.
source: However, more work is needed to characterize the functional effects of these genes, as well as the molecular and evolutionary dynamics between hosts and parasites. For example, if host polymorphism is adaptive, it may not be readily replaced in natural populations.
evidence: Inferred from evolutionary theory about balancing selection

claim: Gene-by-gene interactions between snail and schistosome genotypes could permit the rapid evolution of parasite counterstrategies.
source: Furthermore, gene-by-gene interactions between snail and schistosome genotypes could permit the rapid evolution of parasite counterstrategies.
evidence: Inferred from coevolutionary theory

claim: It is unlikely that a universally resistant snail could be generated by a single genetic change in the context of ancient trench warfare coevolution.
source: In the context of ancient trench warfare coevolution, it is unlikely that a universally resistant snail could be generated by a single genetic change, although successive changes could enhance parasite resistance enough to impact patterns of transmission (Theron et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from coevolutionary theory and supported by citation to Theron et al., 2014

claim: Successive genetic changes could enhance parasite resistance enough to impact patterns of transmission.
source: In the context of ancient trench warfare coevolution, it is unlikely that a universally resistant snail could be generated by a single genetic change, although successive changes could enhance parasite resistance enough to impact patterns of transmission (Theron et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Theron et al., 2014 and inference

claim: Snail TM1 proteins may bind to key schistosome molecules that mediate invasion of the host.
source: As an alternative to genetic modification, future work could leverage the hypothesis that the snail TM1 proteins bind to key schistosome molecules that mediate invasion of the host.
evidence: Inferred from the function of TM1 proteins and their association with resistance

claim: Clusters of immune recognition loci with elevated functional diversity have long been used to track and predict patterns of adaptive variation across populations and species.
source: More broadly, clusters of immune recognition loci with elevated functional diversity have long been used to track and predict patterns of adaptive variation across populations and species (Sommer, 2005; Spurgin and Richardson, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sommer, 2005 and Spurgin and Richardson, 2010

claim: This class of genes (TM1 clusters) will play a central role in disease control as the molecular aspects of vector biology are fully brought to bear on schistosomiasis.
source: Thus, we anticipate that this class of genes will play a central role in disease control as the molecular aspects of vector biology are fully brought to bear on schistosomiasis.
evidence: Inferred from the importance of these genes in resistance and their potential applications

claim: The 13-16-R1 population has been maintained in the absence of parasite exposure.
source: Our population has been maintained in the absence of parasite exposure, and therefore under relaxed selective pressure in regard to parasite resistance.
evidence: Supported by knowledge of laboratory population maintenance

claim: About 40% of 13-16-R1 snails became infected when challenged with PR-1 miracidia.
source: In brief, we arbitrarily chose 1700 outbred juvenile snails (4–6 mm diameter), challenged them each with five miracidia, and classified them as infected or uninfected. About 40% of snails became infected.
evidence: Supported by experimental infection data

claim: Pooled sequencing of 600 infected and 600 uninfected snails achieved 298x and 333x coverage, respectively.
source: In pooled whole-genome sequencing of 600 infected and 600 uninfected 13–16-R1 snails (298x and 333x coverage, respectively), a single genomic region showed by far the greatest difference in allele frequencies between pools (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data

claim: Three PacBio assemblies were generated from inbred snail lines homozygous for the three PTC2 alleles.
source: We generated three PacBio assemblies from inbred snail lines homozygous for the three PTC2 alleles. (Supplementary file 1C; assemblies NCBI Genome, BioProject Accession PRJNA639204).
evidence: Supported by genome assembly data

claim: The homR assembly used snail line R68 and was sequenced in 15 SMRT cells (78x coverage).
source: The first assembly (homR) used snail line R68, which is derived from 13-16-R1 and is highly resistant to S. mansoni strain PR-1, as described previously (Tennessen et al., 2015a). We pooled and sequenced these snails in 15 SMRT cells (78x coverage) on the Pacific Biosciences Sequel I at the CGRB.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data

claim: The homS1 assembly was generated from snail line i90 using 6 SMRT cells (58x coverage).
source: Similarly, the other two assemblies (homS1 and homS2) were generated using the same methodology from snail lines i90 (6 SMRT cells, 58x coverage) and i171 (5 SMRT cells, 46x coverage), respectively.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data

claim: The homS2 assembly was generated from snail line i171 using 5 SMRT cells (46x coverage).
source: Similarly, the other two assemblies (homS1 and homS2) were generated using the same methodology from snail lines i90 (6 SMRT cells, 58x coverage) and i171 (5 SMRT cells, 46x coverage), respectively.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data

claim: 1489 homR contigs were assigned to linkage groups, representing 635 Mb.
source: We thus assigned 1489 homR contigs to linkage groups, representing 635 Mb; these assignments were supported by a median of seven mapped fragments per homR contig, with an average of 96% of fragments per homR contig mapping to the same linkage group.
evidence: Supported by linkage mapping analysis

claim: GRC is also known as PTC1.
source: as GRC (=PTC1) was the first such cluster described in Biomphalaria, we designate this second region as Polymorphic Transmembrane Cluster 2 (PTC2).
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text that GRC equals PTC1
